<h2>SherlockEQ 0.1.0</h2>

<p>
  First public release. SherlockEQ is a per-ear audio equalizer for macOS,
  useful for anyone who wants better control over how their Mac sounds —
  not only listeners with hearing differences or tinnitus. It taps system
  audio through Apple's native Core Audio Tap API. No virtual driver, no
  kernel extension, no audio-routing setup. Use the master gain by itself,
  or layer in audiogram-shaped curves, tinnitus notch filtering, AutoEQ
  headphone correction, and dose tracking — as few or as many features as
  you want.
</p>

<h3>What's in 0.1</h3>

<p><strong>Equalization</strong></p>
<ul>
  <li>Independent left and right EQ chains, implemented as Direct Form II
    Transposed biquad cascades. No AVAudioUnitEQ on the user-signal path —
    real per-channel separation, not coupled stereo processing.</li>
  <li>Four EQ modes per profile: Simple (bass / mid / treble shelves), Speech
    (six speech-frequency bands with presets), Advanced (ten octave-spaced
    parametric bands), and Expert (any band, any frequency, any filter type —
    keyboard-driven).</li>
  <li>AutoEQ headphone correction upstream of the profile EQ. Imports the
    standard ParametricEQ.txt format.</li>
  <li>Master output gain with a dedicated post-limiter stage (-60 dB to +24 dB)
    and per-profile stereo balance.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Tinnitus</strong></p>
<ul>
  <li>Continuous-phase sine sweep across 20 Hz to 20 kHz, fine-tunable to
    one hertz.</li>
  <li>Per-ear notch filtering. Set the tone for the left ear, the right ear,
    or both.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Audiogram</strong></p>
<ul>
  <li>Per-ear threshold entry on a log-frequency chart.</li>
  <li>Translated into an EQ curve in real time with severity bars and a
    live preview.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Safety</strong></p>
<ul>
  <li>NIOSH dose tracking with a remaining-time readout smoothed over short
    transients (60-second EMA in the power domain).</li>
  <li>Per-frequency safety overlay on the spectrum, calibration-aware.</li>
  <li>Menu-bar dose tint and notifications at warning and danger thresholds.</li>
  <li>Apple AUPeakLimiter on the output bus.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Workflow</strong></p>
<ul>
  <li>Menu-bar popover with master gain, balance, profile picker, level
    meters, and a reference-mode bypass.</li>
  <li>Main window with profile management, audiogram entry, four EQ surfaces,
    tinnitus tone finder, safe listening dashboard, and a persistent
    right-side monitor sidebar.</li>
  <li>Profile import and export. Undo and redo with per-band coalescing.</li>
  <li>Built-in profiles cannot be edited; duplicate to customize.</li>
  <li>Device auto-switch when a profile is linked to an output.</li>
</ul>

<p><strong>Accessibility</strong></p>
<ul>
  <li>VoiceOver and keyboard control across every custom canvas and drag
    surface, including audiogram entry, EQ band sliders, and the tinnitus
    sweep.</li>
  <li>Color-blind redundant encoding on safety zones (icon plus position,
    not just color).</li>
  <li>Reduced-motion guards on transitions. Dynamic Type respected on
    labels.</li>
</ul>

<h3>What's not in 0.1</h3>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Onboarding wizard.</strong> First launch goes straight to the
    main UI; you will be prompted for Microphone and Screen &amp; System
    Audio Recording permissions cold. The second prompt is non-obvious —
    macOS requires it for any system-audio capture. SherlockEQ does not
    record video or screen contents.</li>
  <li><strong>Localization beyond English.</strong> The String Catalog
    infrastructure is in place; translations are not yet wired.</li>
  <li><strong>Spectrogram visualization.</strong> Code is present but
    disabled pending a performance and UX revision.</li>
</ul>

<h3>Requirements</h3>

<ul>
  <li>macOS 14.6 or later</li>
  <li>Apple Silicon or Intel (universal binary)</li>
  <li>Microphone permission and Screen &amp; System Audio Recording permission</li>
</ul>

<h3>Not a medical device</h3>

<p>
  SherlockEQ is not a healthcare or medical application. It does not diagnose,
  treat, measure, or monitor any hearing condition, tinnitus, or disability.
  For concerns about your hearing, consult a doctor, audiologist, or licensed
  healthcare professional.
</p>
